title: Save points with Git
hook: Keep every version of your work and put it online.

warmup.q: Yesterday: a response comes back with status 404. What does that mean?
warmup.explain: 404 means not found. 200 is all good and 500 means the other computer broke.

options: Adds to the end of the file and keeps what is already there
Wipes the file and starts again
warmup.explain: "a" is append: new text goes on the end. "w" wipes first, and "r" only reads.

warmup.q: `for i in range(1, 4):` runs the loop with i equal to...
warmup.explain: range stops BEFORE the end number. `range(1, 4)` gives 1, 2 and 3.

why.heading: The final_v2_REAL_final problem
why.text: You know the mess: `edit_final.prproj`, `edit_final2.prproj`, `edit_REAL_final.prproj`. Code is the same. **Git** solves it. It remembers every version of your project, so you can go back to any of them and nothing is ever lost.

why.heading: A commit is a save point
why.text:
A **commit** is a snapshot of your whole folder with a short message, like `Add crew list`. Think of a game save. Three words to know:

`git add` picks what goes in the snapshot
`git commit` takes it
`git push` sends it online

why.heading: GitHub is the online home
why.text: **GitHub** is a website that stores your Git history. It is a backup if your laptop dies, and it is how you show your work to other people, like a showreel for code. A project folder tracked by Git is called a **repository**, or repo.

why.heading: .gitignore and README
why.text: A file called `.gitignore` lists what Git must skip: huge videos, passwords, the `.venv` folder. A file called `README.md` is the front page of your repo: what it is and how to run it. Both are plain text files. You can already write them.

why.heading: Today
why.text: In the browser you build small tools that do what Git does: write a README, and filter a file list the way `.gitignore` does. At the PC you do the real thing: your first commit and push.

watch.intro: This is a tiny pretend `git log`: a list of save points. A commit adds a new one to the end and never changes the old ones.
watch.code:
log = [{"id": "a1f", "msg": "First call sheet"}]
print("Before:")
for c in log:
    print(c["id"], c["msg"])

log.append({"id": "b2c", "msg": "Add crew list"})
print("After one commit:")
for c in log:
    print(c["id"], c["msg"])
explain: Each save point is a dictionary with an id and a message.
`append` adds the new one at the end. The first one is still there.
Real Git does the same, but it saves the whole folder each time.
watch.break_it: Change `c["msg"]` in the first loop to `c["message"]` and tap Run. You get KeyError: 'message'. Change it back.

tasks.title: Write a README
tasks.task:
Ask for the project name. Then write a file called `README.md` with three lines: `# ` and the name, an empty line, then `Made with Python.` For the name `Call Sheet Maker` the file holds:

`# Call Sheet Maker`
``
`Made with Python.`
tasks.starter:
name = input("Project name? ")
with open("README.md", "w") as f:
    f.write("Hello\n")
tasks.solution:
name = input("Project name? ")
with open("README.md", "w") as f:
    f.write(f"# {name}\n\nMade with Python.\n")
hints: Change what goes inside f.write(...). It must be an f-string so the name can go in.
Use \n for a new line. Two \n in a row make the empty line.

expect_files.README.md:
# Call Sheet Maker

Made with Python.

tasks.title: Like .gitignore
tasks.task: `.gitignore` is a file of names Git must skip. `all_files.txt` lists the files in a project. Print every file that is NOT ignored, one per line, in the original order.
tasks.starter:
with open(".gitignore") as f:
    ignored = f.read().split()
with open("all_files.txt") as f:
    names = f.read().split()
# print each name that is NOT in ignored
tasks.solution:
with open(".gitignore") as f:
    ignored = f.read().split()
with open("all_files.txt") as f:
    names = f.read().split()
for name in names:
    if name not in ignored:
        print(name)
hints: Loop over names. For each one, check whether it is in the ignored list.
`if name not in ignored:` is the check. Print the name inside it.

tasks.title: Star rules
tasks.task:
Real `.gitignore` files also have rules like `*.mp4`, which means every file ending in `.mp4`. A file is ignored if its name is listed, OR if `*` plus its suffix is listed (`Path(name).suffix` gives `.mp4`). Print each kept file as `Tracked: name`, then how many were ignored. Example:

`Tracked: main.py`
`Tracked: README.md`
`Tracked: notes.txt`
`Ignored: 3`
tasks.starter:
from pathlib import Path

with open(".gitignore") as f:
    ignored = f.read().split()
with open("all_files.txt") as f:
    names = f.read().split()

skipped = 0
for name in names:
    # ignored if the name is listed, or "*" + suffix is listed
    print("Tracked:", name)
print("Ignored:", skipped)
tasks.solution:
from pathlib import Path

with open(".gitignore") as f:
    ignored = f.read().split()
with open("all_files.txt") as f:
    names = f.read().split()

skipped = 0
for name in names:
    star = "*" + Path(name).suffix
    if name in ignored or star in ignored:
        skipped += 1
    else:
        print("Tracked:", name)
print("Ignored:", skipped)
hints: Make star = "*" + Path(name).suffix inside the loop. For clip1.mp4 that gives *.mp4.
If name in ignored or star in ignored: add 1 to skipped. Otherwise print the Tracked line.
Only the else branch prints. The if branch just does skipped += 1.

files.all_files.txt: main.py clip1.mp4 README.md secrets.txt b-roll.mov notes.txt

tests.expect:
Tracked: main.py
Tracked: README.md
Tracked: notes.txt
Ignored: 3

recap: Git remembers every version of your project. A commit is a save point with a message.
add picks the files, commit takes the snapshot, push sends it to GitHub.
`.gitignore` lists what Git skips: videos, passwords, the .venv folder.
A README is the front page of your repo. You can write one with a program.

words.meaning: A tool that remembers every version of your project.
A save point of your whole folder, with a short message.
A project folder that Git is tracking. Also called a repo.
A website that stores your repos online.
Send your new commits up to GitHub.
The front page file of a repo.

pc.title: First commit and push
pc.why: Your work is only safe and shareable once it is in Git and on GitHub. You make a tiny repo today so the steps are familiar before the capstone.
steps: Open VS Code, then Terminal, New Terminal. Type `git --version` and press Enter. You should see `git version 2` and numbers. If it says not recognised, close VS Code completely and open it again, then retry.

Tell Git who you are, once only. Type `git config --global user.name "Your Name"` and press Enter. Then `git config --global user.email "you@example.com"` using the email on your GitHub account. Nothing is printed when it works.
Make a project folder: click File, Open Folder, open Python 30 Work, click New Folder in the window, name it `hello-git`, then click Select Folder. Click Yes if it asks you to trust it.
Open a new terminal (Terminal, New Terminal). The last line should end with `hello-git>`. If not, close the terminal with the bin icon and open another.

Make three files with the New File icon in the left panel. Name them `README.md` (type `# Hello Git` inside), `hello.py` (type `print("Hello from Git")`) and `.gitignore` (type `.venv/` on line one and `secrets.txt` on line two). Press Ctrl+S in each.
Type `git init` and press Enter. It says `Initialized empty Git repository`. Then type `git branch -M main` and press Enter (nothing is printed).
Type `git status` and press Enter. Your three files show in red under Untracked. Red means Git sees them but is not saving them yet.
Type `git add .` and press Enter (the dot means everything). A line-endings warning may appear: ignore it. Type `git status` again: the files are now green.
Type `git commit -m "First commit"` and press Enter. It says `3 files changed`. If it says Please tell me who you are, redo step 2.

Open github.com in your browser and sign in. Click the plus at the top right, then New repository. Name it `hello-git`, pick Public, do NOT tick any boxes to add a README or .gitignore, then click Create repository.

GitHub shows a page with commands. Find the box that says push an existing repository from the command line. Copy its two lines (`git remote add origin ...` and `git push -u origin main`) and paste them into the VS Code terminal, one at a time, pressing Enter after each.
A window may pop up asking you to sign in to GitHub. Click Sign in with your browser and approve. The push ends with `branch 'main' set up to track 'origin/main'`.
Refresh the GitHub page. Your three files are there and the README is shown as the front page.

Make a second save point: change the text in hello.py, press Ctrl+S, then type `git add .`, `git commit -m "Change greeting"`, `git push`. Refresh GitHub and click the Commits link to see both save points.
